body:
The maintainer reported this in chat on 2026-11-14:

> on the WCS page - under Quarter turns - there should be a "flip X", "flip Y" and "flip Z" button.. and what that does is flipping X+ to X- direction and vice versa for the other direction - without turning the gizmo around nother axis. As some machine has their directions reversed...

Expected: three buttons, `Flip X`, `Flip Y` and `Flip Z`, are below Quarter turns on the WCS page. Each button reverses the direction of one WCS axis. The other two axes do not move.

Open design points:
- A flip of one axis makes a left-handed frame. A rotation quaternion cannot store it. The WCS needs a sign for each axis, or an equivalent record, in the project file.
- A flip changes the sign of posted coordinates on that axis. It also changes arc direction (`G2`/`G3`), cutter compensation side (`G41`/`G42`) and the climb or conventional sense. The post must write these correctly, or refuse the program with a named reason.
- Simulation and the gouge checks must use the same frame as the post.
- The gizmo must show the flipped axis.

Each flip is an undoable command. It ships with an MCP tool, or a follow-up `MCP:` issue names it.

Effort is `effort:high` because the change can alter posted G-code (safety floor).

Done means: the three buttons are on the WCS page, each flip is one undo step, the project file keeps the flips, and golden NC tests pin the posted output of a flipped axis, with arcs and cutter compensation.

body:
Found while fixing #1532.

What happens: with the new Between setups option (default Pause), the program writes an M0 (or M1) after each setup's last operation. Fanuc and Tormach PathPilot also lift Z clear first and write a comment naming the next setup, read from the new `PARAM SetupChange "<setup>"` record. The other dialects that declare `afterModes` (Haas, Mazak, Doosan DNM, Sinumerik, Heidenhain, grblHAL, TinyG, the lathe and wire posts) ignore that record: they write the stop where they write an operator's own stop, with no Z lift and no comment, so the operator gets a bare stop with the tool at clearance height and no word on what to do.

Expected: each afterModes dialect reads `SetupChange` and, at a setup-change stop, lifts Z by its own retract (the one it uses before a tool change) and writes a comment (or its message form) naming the next setup, as `assets/posts/fanuc.cps` and `assets/posts/tormach.cps` do.

Evidence: `crates/app/tests/between_setups.rs` pins Fanuc and Tormach only; `crates/app/src/posting_setup_change.rs` writes the record for every post.

Done means: every built-in afterModes mill dialect writes the Z lift and the next-setup comment before a setup-change stop, each pinned by a post test; lathe and wire dialects either do the same or are named in the issue as not applicable.

title: macOS: sign and notarize the release app so Gatekeeper opens it without a workaround

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: area:build
labels.description: Build, CI, release, tests

labels.name: effort:medium
labels.description: One module or crate, a known pattern (issue-worker-medium)

labels.name: P6
labels.description: Accepted enhancement, not scheduled

body:
### What are you trying to do

Open CamCraft on a Mac after downloading it from the releases page, without having to override Gatekeeper.

The macOS app is ad-hoc signed and not notarized (`scripts/package-macos.sh`: "Distribution signing and notarization can replace this when credentials exist"). A browser download gets the quarantine flag, and macOS then blocks the first launch because Apple can't verify the developer. Every new release is a new copy, so a user has to override Gatekeeper again after each update.

The README says the first launch "may require Control-click → Open". Since macOS 15 (Sequoia) that no longer works for an app that isn't notarized: the user has to try to open it, then go to System Settings › Privacy & Security and click Open Anyway, or run `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/CamCraft.app` in Terminal.

### How you imagine it working

The release signs the macOS app with a Developer ID certificate and notarizes it, so it opens like any other downloaded app. It would work the same way Windows signing does now (`scripts/sign.ps1`):

- `scripts/package-macos.sh` signs with Developer ID (hardened runtime, secure timestamp) when signing credentials are configured through the environment, and keeps today's ad-hoc signature, with a printed "unsigned" line, when they aren't. Unsigned stays a valid release.
- When credentials are configured, the release job submits the ZIP or DMG with `xcrun notarytool submit --wait`, then staples the ticket to the app and the DMG with `xcrun stapler staple`.
- The certificate and the notary credentials (an App Store Connect API key, or an Apple ID with an app-specific password) live in repository secrets, as the Windows PFX does.

This needs an Apple Developer Program membership, so whether and when to do it is the maintainer's call. A smaller step that helps meanwhile: update the README's macOS line to the macOS 15 steps above.

title: A part-source cross drill is not judged against the setup's other parts (#1621's neighbour law skips it)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: P1
labels.description: Unsafe or wrong output: gouge, collision, wrong G-code, crash, data loss; blocks a cut

labels.name: area:2d
labels.description: 2D milling

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Found while fixing #1635 (PR #1640). I read this from the code and have not reproduced it with a run.

**What happens.** #1621 judges a part-source operation against the setup's OTHER parts (`keep_law::neighbour_parts`). It does so only for kinds that carry a part law, i.e. `depth_law_of(params, src, true)` is not `None`. A Drill with cross holes reads `DepthLaw::None`, so `neighbour_parts` is empty for it. Its chain answers only to `cross_part` against its own source's mesh, and since #1640 also against the setup's parts when the source is the stock.

So a cross hole drilled on part B, from a raw stock that also holds part A, whose drill or approach enters A, may carry no finding on the op. The program sim refuses to judge a posed (radial) chain, so whether such a program then posts is the open question.

**Expected.** A part-source cross drill that enters a neighbouring part is a blocking finding on the op, or is refused by name.

Done means:
- a test with a part-source cross drill on B entering a neighbouring part A is refused or blocked;
- the same drill clear of A still posts.

Part of the #1621 / #1635 part laws.

body:
Found while fixing #1631 (PR #1634). Read from the code; not reproduced by a run yet.

What happens: #1631 gives a stock-source Drill (no cross holes), Bore and Thread the containment law against the setup's parts (`keep_law::is_hole_kind`, `parts_in_stock`). A Drill WITH cross holes is left out. Its chain is judged by `cross_part::part_clear`, which reads `material.facets`, the source's mesh (`generate.rs`, the `cross_spindle::cross_drill` call). On a stock source that is the stock, not the parts held in it. So a cross hole off the stock that enters a part may have no op finding. The cross chain is posed, so the program sim refuses to judge it. Whether such a program then posts, or is refused another way (the stock read as the solid to keep), is the open question.

Expected: a stock-source cross drill that enters a part is a blocking finding on the op, or is refused by name. A cross hole through stock-only material, or into a cross hole the part models, stays legal.

Open design point: the containment law in `contain_into` excuses vertical hole walls only (`HoleAxis::vertical`). A cross chain needs each hole's own axis, as `cross_part::walls` builds them.

Done means: a test with a stock-source cross drill into a part, and one into stock-only material, shows a blocking finding or a named refusal for the first, and the second still posts or is refused only for a stated reason.

Part of the #1607 / #1631 stock-source law.

body:
Split from #1616. PR #1632 fixes grblHAL, TinyG and Carvera; this issue is the rest.

**What happens.** fanuc.cps, haas.cps, mazak.cps, doosan-dnm.cps, sinumerik.cps and heidenhain.cps write the stream's first rapid after the tool change and `G43 H..` as one combined move: `G00 X20 Y10 Z-3`. That is a straight line from wherever the tool change left the spindle. It is safe only while that start height is above the part. With a tool too long for the work offset, the line starts below the part top and crosses it. This is the hazard of #1614, which a PathPilot Hub run found on Tormach.

**Expected.** Before its first X/Y traverse after each tool change (and at program start), each post states the section's clearance Z as a Z-only rapid: `ClearancePlane`, else `RetractPlane`, never below the move's own Z. A stream that states neither plane is refused by name. Use the wording of #1618 (Tormach) and #1632 (grblHAL, TinyG, Carvera) so all the posts read alike.

**Care points.**
- These posts carry G43.4 (TCP) and rotary paths. The Z-only rapid must be in the right frame for each of them, or refused there by name.
- About 100 goldens and two dozen test files read these posts. Every moved golden must be checked by diff, and only the expected one-line insertion may move.
- Widen the `assets/posts/AGENTS.md` bullet that #1618 adds to name every post.

**Done means:** each of the six posts writes the clearance Z before its first X/Y traverse after a tool change; a stream with no stated plane is refused by name; pinned per post with mutation checks; moved goldens listed in the PR.

body:
Found while reviewing PR 1622 (the stock-source law of issue 1607). Read from the code and the PR body; not reproduced by a run yet.

What happens: PR 1622 gives a 2D operation whose source is the stock a part law for the pocket family, Slot, Trochoidal slot, Circular, Contour, Face, Engrave and Trace (`keep_law::is_stock_kept_kind`). 2D Chamfer and the hole kinds (Drill, Bore, Thread) on a stock source stay at `DepthLaw::None`; the PR body says so under "not exercised" ("not in #1607's list; the chamfer's depth is derived and its break is credited only on the part, the hole kinds would need modelled hole rims excused"). Such an operation that cuts into a part standing in the stock has no operation finding. On an aligned stock the program simulation can still hold it; on a turned stock the simulation refuses to judge, so the program posts.

Expected: a cut into a held part is a blocking finding on the operation whatever its kind, or the post is refused by name where no law can judge it (Prime Directive: correct, or visibly refused).

Evidence: `crates/app/src/operation/keep_law.rs` (`is_stock_kept_kind`, `parts_in_stock`), `depth_law_of`, `run_job` in `crates/app/src/operation/generate.rs` at PR 1622 head c74d888d; the same holds on main, where no stock-source kind outside the pocket family is judged.

Open design points: what a chamfer's break may remove on a stock source; how a drilled or bored hole's own rim in the part is excused without excusing a hole through a neighbouring part.

Done means: a test per kind (Chamfer, Drill, Bore, Thread) with a stock source and a part in the cut, on an aligned and on a turned stock, shows a blocking finding or a named post refusal; a legal case of each kind still posts.

title: An op judged against parts beside its source does not read Stale when one of them moves

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: P1
labels.description: Unsafe or wrong output: gouge, collision, wrong G-code, crash, data loss; blocks a cut

labels.name: area:2d
labels.description: 2D milling

labels.name: area:sim
labels.description: Stock simulation and verification

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
**What happens:** since #1603 (stock-source pocket family), #1607 (every stock-source 2D kind with a part law) and #1621 (a part-source op against the setup's other parts, PR #1622), an operation's verdict is read against parts BESIDE its source (`keep_law::parts_in_stock`, `keep_law::neighbour_parts`). The op's stamp (`operation::stamp::current_stamp`) still digests only the source (plus the stock for a non-stock source). So after a clean generation, a part that is moved into the cut, added, un-tagged as a fixture, or un-marked as raw stock only leaves the op `Ok` with a verdict nobody gave.

- Aligned stock: the program sim judges every part live at post and refuses.
- **Turned stock** (the sim refuses to judge): the post reads the ops' cached verdicts - all `Ok` and clean - and the program goes out into the moved part. Same hole the original #1603 / #1607 / #1621 fixes closed, re-opened by an edit after generation.

The other direction is fail-safe but confusing: marking a casting raw stock only (#1094) or moving a neighbour away leaves the op `Ok` with its old gouges cached; the post refuses until the user regenerates for no visible reason.

**Tried on PR #1622 and pulled back** (branch `issue/1607-stock-source-law`: f4d86b41 and 6abccc77 add it, the commit after dae97790 takes it out again): a stamp term digesting the kept set (`name`, `setup_align::pose_in`, `model::geometry_signature` of each model the part laws read; written only when the set is non-empty). It works (pinned: moving the neighbour makes the op Stale; red without the term), but it breaks established stamp contracts that need a maintainer's call:
- `fixtures.rs::workholding_never_stales_a_fresh_toolpath` - un-tagging a vise turns it into a part, so the op goes Stale (the "workholding never stales" law, M2.3).
- `operations.rs::a_frommodel_stock_survives_its_source_being_deleted` and `a_model_update_does_not_touch_a_box_stock` - "a stock-based path never reads the model": a stock-source Face now does (its parts).
- `fidelity_copies.rs` (2 tests) - deleting the stock's coarse source model makes the stock-source op Stale, so the gate says "regenerate" instead of the named fidelity refusal.
- `stock_source_verdict.rs` - marking the casting raw stock only stales a part-source op.

**Options:** (a) the stamp term above, restating those contracts (the kept parts are inputs; workholding stays out only while it is tagged); (b) no stamp term, but the post re-reads the part laws live for ops whose kept set changed (like the workholding gate does), so nothing churns; (c) (b) only when the sim cannot judge.

Found while fixing #1621 (PR #1622; `docs/decisions/1607-stock-source-law.md`).

Done means: a part moved into a stock-source or part-source op's cut after generation never posts on a turned stock (refused by name, Stale or live re-judgement); the chosen option's contract changes are decided and recorded; pinned and mutation-checked.

body:
**What happens:** `mark_law::budget_of` declares a mark for an Engrave or Trace, and `stock_sim::credit_marks` credits that budget against every part the setup holds (`setup_align::parts_facets_in`). A part-source mark on part B whose flank enters a neighbouring part A by its depth is therefore credited on A too and passes the program sim.

Measured on #1621's probe (B the #1585 pocket block on x [0, 40], A a 40 x 40 x 8 box on x [-40, -0.7], 80 x 80 x 8 stock, EM-0600-4FL): a 0.3 mm Trace / Engrave round B, its flank 2.3 mm x 0.3 mm into A, **posted on the aligned stock** before #1621.

**Why it is P7, not P1:** since #1621 (PR #1622) the operation itself judges A with the plain solid law (no budget) and refuses the cut on both stocks, so no wrong program posts. The two judges disagree only in the sim's direction (looser) on a neighbour.

**Expected:** the sim credits a mark only on the part(s) the operation marks (its source's entities for a part source; every part for a stock source, where the op's own law reads them all), so the sim agrees with the op.

**Where:** `crates/app/src/stock_sim_marks.rs`, `crates/sim/src/stock_sim/mark.rs` (`credit_marks`), `crates/app/src/operation/mark_law.rs` (`budget_of`).

Found while fixing #1621 (PR #1622; `docs/decisions/1607-stock-source-law.md`, #1621 section).

Done means: the #1621 probe with the op's neighbour law disabled is refused by the program sim on the aligned stock; a legal mark on B still posts; pinned and mutation-checked.

title: Tormach post: a section that keeps its tool still runs G30 (Z dips to the stored G30 height, then lifts again)

labels.name: effort:max

body:
Seen in the #1614 Hub run (770MX sim, 2026-11-13). The tool was already in the spindle. The program still ran `G53 G0 Z0` / `G30` / `T4 M6` / `G43 H4` / `G53 G0 Z0`. Hub's stored G30 Z sits about 0.9" below the top of travel, so Z went up, dipped to the G30 height, and went straight back up (the #1596 re-lift) before the clearance move. It is safe (the G30 height was about 3" above the part), but the user found it odd, and it is wasted motion.

**Proposed fix:** when the stream's TOOL is the one already loaded, `tormach.cps` skips the G30 and M6 (keeping the G43 and the lift). Check how PathPilot treats an `M6` for the tool already in the spindle before relying on that. Note that at the program start the post cannot know what is loaded, so the first tool change of a program keeps its G30.

**Done means:** a repeated tool number in the same program posts no second G30 / M6. That is pinned by a test, and the moved goldens are listed in the PR.

Related: #1614 (PR #1618), #1596.

title: Clippy 1.100 on the runner fails camcraft-geometry: needless_range_loop x3 in feature.rs

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: P2
labels.description: Main is broken or a regression with no workaround; blocks a cut

labels.name: area:3d
labels.description: 3D milling and finishing

labels.name: area:build
labels.description: Build, CI, release, tests

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:low
labels.description: Mechanical, one file, no new logic (issue-worker-low)

body:
What happens: the "Clippy on the touched crates" step of `pr-test.yml` fails on the self-hosted runner for any PR that touches `camcraft-geometry`, with three `needless_range_loop` errors ("loop variable `slot` is only used to index `e.facets`") in `crates/geometry/src/geometry/feature.rs` at lines 481, 1205 and 1486. The lines are not part of the PR that hit it.

Evidence:
- Run 43546645706 (PR 1576, head `e7d78efe`, runner `uma`): clippy step red with the three errors above. The log's help links point at `rust-1.100.0`.
- Main at `c00ba18a9`, local Windows machine, rustc 1.99.0 / clippy 0.1.99: `cargo clippy -p camcraft-geometry --all-targets -- -D warnings` exits 0 with no lints.
- So the runner's newer clippy (1.100) fires a lint the local 1.99 does not. No toolchain file pins the version, so runner and contributors can differ.

Not verified: that the three lines are byte-identical on main and on PR 1576's head (the PR's reviewer read them as untouched by the PR).

Expected: the same clippy verdict on the runner and locally, and a green clippy step for a PR that did not touch the flagged lines.

Suggested fix (either or both):
- Rewrite the three loops as iterator loops (`for (slot, f) in e.facets.iter().enumerate()` or the form clippy suggests), with no behaviour change. This is geometry code, so the change is read with care and the feature suites run.
- Decide whether the toolchain is pinned (a `rust-toolchain.toml` is a file `pr-test.yml` refuses in a PR diff, so that part is the maintainer's decision).

Done means: `cargo clippy -p camcraft-geometry --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean on clippy 1.100 and 1.99, and the clippy step of a `pr-test.yml` run on a geometry-touching PR is green.

body:
**What happens:** the laws a 2D operation carries on a part source (`Mark` for Engrave / Trace, `Keep` for the whole-model pocket family, `Section` for picks) read only the **source entity's** mesh. When the setup holds a second part and the cut on part B reaches into part A, the operation has no finding for A. With the stock aligned the program sim blocks the post; with the stock **turned** (the sim refuses to judge) nothing judges A.

Found by M5's review of PR #1615 (pullrequestreview-5900976523, note 2): two parts side by side, a Trace on B whose flank runs 2.3 mm into the taller part A:

| stock | result |
|---|---|
| aligned | the program sim refuses (worst 2.00 mm) |
| turned 90 deg about Z | the op records **no Gouge for A** (in that probe the post was blocked only by an unrelated rapid) |

It predates #1615 and applies equally to `Section`-law kinds on B.

**Expected:** a part-source 2D operation is judged against every part the setup holds, not only the one its source names: its own law against its source (unchanged), and the plain solid law against the setup's other parts (`setup_align::parts_facets_in`, the mesh the program sim judges against; fixtures and a stock-only model left out). A cut into a neighbour is a blocking `Warning::Gouge` on the move on both stocks.

**Where:** `crates/app/src/operation/job.rs` (`keep_parts`, today filled only for a stock source by `keep_law::parts_in_stock`) and the two frame arms of `run_job` in `generate.rs`. #1607 widens `keep_parts` to every 2D kind on a **stock** source on top of PR #1615's branch; this is the same mechanism for a **part** source, so it should stack on #1607 (or land after it) rather than touch those lines in parallel. For Engrave / Trace the neighbour gets no mark budget (the mark is on the source part); note that the sim's mark credit currently holds a neighbour to the budget, so the operation would be the stricter judge there.

**Done means:** the two-part probe above is refused on the operation by name on both stocks, for Engrave, Trace and one `Section` kind; a legal cut on B that stays clear of A still posts on both; pinned through generate and the post, mutation-checked; decision recorded.

Related: #1595, #1603, #1607, PR #1615 (`docs/decisions/1595-engrave-mark-law.md`, "Notes for the maintainer").

title: Mill posts: the first traverse after a tool change does not state its clearance Z (grblhal, carvera; fanuc-family combined first rapid)

labels.name: P1

labels.name: area:post
labels.description: Post processors and G-code

labels.name: in-review

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Found while fixing #1614, the same hazard in the other mill posts.

**The hazard (#1614, from a PathPilot Hub run).** After a tool change the spindle stands at the top of Z travel. With a long tool on a high work offset, the tip can stand below the part top there. A first X/Y move that does not first state a clearance height then crosses the part. `tormach.cps` now writes `G0 Z<ClearancePlane>` (else the `RetractPlane`) before the first X/Y traverse. A setup that cannot clear is then stopped by the control's Z limit, not rapided through the part. A stream that states neither plane is refused by name.

**Same pattern elsewhere** (from the synth goldens, `crates/app/tests/golden/nc/synth_*.nc`):
- `grblhal.cps`, `carvera.cps`: `T2 M6` ... `G0 X20 Y10` is a bare X/Y traverse at whatever height the tool change left, then `G0 X20 Y10 Z-3`. This is exactly the #1614 shape.
- `fanuc.cps`, `haas.cps`, `mazak.cps`, `doosan-dnm.cps`, `sinumerik.cps`, `heidenhain.cps`: after `G43 H..`, the first block is the stream's first rapid as one combined move, `G00 X20 Y10 Z-3`. It goes in a straight line from the tool-change height. It is safe only while that start height is above the part. With a tool too long for the work offset, the line starts below the part top.
- `tinyg.cps`: check it too (it lifts with `G53 G0 Z0` after `M0`, then traverses).

**Done means:** each spindle mill post states the section's clearance Z (a Z-only rapid to `ClearancePlane`, else `RetractPlane`) before its first X/Y motion after a tool change and at the program start. A stream stating neither is refused by name. There is a pinning test per post. Moved goldens are regenerated and listed in the PR (expect one added `G0 Z` line per program, as #1614 saw across 32 Tormach goldens).

Part of the #1614 follow-up.

What happens: opening a project resets the open document before the new file is parsed. A `.camproj` that is valid text but bad JSON (or otherwise fails to load) therefore leaves the user with an empty document: the old one is gone and the new one did not load. Only a non-text file is refused before the reset. Both paths do it: the disk open and the browser byte open (`open_project_bytes`, PR 1314).

Expected: a project that cannot be loaded changes nothing. Parse and check the new file first; replace the open document only when the load succeeded.

Evidence: found by reading in the review of PR 1314 (its body says a refused project "changes nothing", which holds for a non-text file only). Not reproduced by running the app.

Priority note: rated P3 because Open replaces the document anyway when it succeeds; raise it if unsaved work is lost without the unsaved-changes prompt.

Done means: a test opens a corrupt project over a document with content, on the disk path and the byte path, and the document, its history and its file name are unchanged; the refusal names the file.

body:
**What happens:** a 2D operation whose source is the **stock** (or a pick off the setup's stock) carries no part law on the operation (`part_solid` is false, so `depth_law_of` returns `DepthLaw::None` before the kind's arm). When the stock holds a part and the cut reaches into it, the operation has 0 findings. With the stock aligned the program sim blocks the post; with the stock **turned** (the sim refuses to judge) the post goes out.

Found while working #1595 / #1603 (branch `issue/1595-engrave-law`, upstream main 745edc36 plus that branch).

**Probe:** the #1585 fixture (40 x 40 x 8 block, R15 pocket to Z4, EM-0600-4FL) in a 40 x 40 x 8 box stock centred over it. Engrave / Trace, source `Stock`, Top Z8, Bottom Z1 (the stock's outline is the part's outline, so the line runs down the part's outside wall):

| kind | op findings | stock aligned | stock turned 90 deg about Z |
|---|---|---|---|
| Engrave | 0 | blocked by the program sim ("worst 7.00 mm") | **posts** |
| Trace | 0 | blocked by the program sim ("worst 7.00 mm") | **posts** |

The same holds by construction for the other kinds that are judged only on a part source: Slot, Trochoidal slot, Circular (`authored_law`), Contour and Face (`Section`). #1593 pinned the stock-source Trochoidal slot as never judged (`a_trochoid_on_the_stock_is_never_judged`); these were not probed here.

**What #1603's fix covers and what it leaves:** the pocket family (2D Pocket, 2D Adaptive, 2D Offset) on a stock source is now judged against the setup's parts (`operation::keep_law::parts_in_stock`, the mesh the program sim judges against). The job carries those parts only for that family. Every other kind on a stock source is still unjudged on the operation.

**Expected:** a stock-source operation in a setup that holds a part is judged against that part by the law its kind takes on a part source (Mark for Engrave / Trace, with the sim's mark credit extended to match; Section for the typed kinds, Contour and Face), or the decision that the stock source is never judged is restated with a refusal where the program sim cannot judge. Either way the aligned and the turned stock give the same verdict.

**Not simply `uncovered()`:** refusing every None-law op when the sim cannot judge would refuse a legal stock-source Face on any turned stock (see `docs/decisions/1595-engrave-mark-law.md`).

**Done means:** the probe rows above are refused on the operation by name (or the post is blocked) on both stocks; a legal stock-source cut that stays off the part (a Face above it, a Contour round the stock) still posts on both; `a_trochoid_on_the_stock_is_never_judged` is kept or replaced by a stated decision; pinned through generate and the post, mutation-checked.

Related: #1603, #1595, #1593, #1554.

body:
**What happens:** whole-model 2D Pocket and 2D Adaptive (and the stock-source Adaptive of #1554) can cut into the part with **no finding on the op**. On a **turned (rotated) stock** the post goes out, because the program sim refuses to judge a turned stock and nothing else catches it. Found by M5's review of PR #1597 (pullrequestreview-5899991928), on upstream main be27a4c7 plus #1597.

| Case | Depth into the part | Op findings | Aligned stock | Turned stock |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pocket / Adaptive2D, whole-model source, Area offset +3 | 4.0-4.25 mm | 0 | blocked by the program sim | **posts** |
| Pocket / Adaptive2D, whole-model source, extension +5 | 5 mm | 0 | blocked by the program sim | **posts** |
| #1554: stock-source Adaptive2D / Pocket | 7 mm | 0 | blocked by the program sim | **posts** |

With default area controls (and containment On or Outside) these ops stay outside the part (worst clearance -0.005 mm). The gouge needs a positive area offset or extension, or a stock source.

**Why:** these ops carry `DepthLaw::None`, so the op itself never judges the cut against the model. `uncovered()` (crates/app/src/posting_sim.rs) counts any fresh, stamped op as judged whatever its depth law, so when the program sim cannot model the stock (turned, posed, rotary), a None-law op that cuts the part goes to the post. Same root as #1595 (Engrave/Trace) and the TrochoidalSlot gap fixed by #1597. This is a gouge that passes on a turned stock: P1.

**Expected:** a whole-model or stock-source Pocket or Adaptive2D whose cut reaches into the part is refused on the op by name (a law that judges the region it actually cuts against the model), or at minimum `uncovered()` refuses to post a None-law op on a model source when the program sim cannot judge it. Legal whole-model pockets with default controls must still post. That is why #1597 did not simply make `uncovered()` refuse every None-law op.

**Done means:** the three rows above are refused (on the op, and the post is blocked) with the stock aligned and turned; legal whole-model pockets and adaptives with default controls still post on both. Pinned through `operation::generate` and the post, mutation-checked.

Related: #1595 (the same `uncovered()` question for Engrave/Trace), #1554 (stock-source Adaptive: not only verify-caught; it posts on a turned stock), #1593 / PR #1597, #1550.

body:
## What happens

Two AP214 part files from the user (`10208.STEP`, `32050.STEP`; not attached — they are the user's, available on request) do not import, on the head of PR #1576 (bda36c6e, which carries #1574 and #1573's closed-shell check), debug `camcraft-cli script` → `cam.import`:

| File | Faces | Surfaces | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `10208.STEP` | 67 in 2 `MANIFOLD_SOLID_BREP` / `CLOSED_SHELL` | 31 cylinder, 12 cone, 19 plane, 2 sphere, 3 rational B-spline | **refused after 588 s, 2.3 GB RSS**: `closed shell #1319 (52 faces) meshes open: 13227 unmatched edges, the first from (4.8174, 4.1370, -6.7542) to (5.1105, 3.7690, -6.7776) mm` |
| `32050.STEP` | 101 in 2 solids | 52 cylinder, 13 cone, 33 plane, 3 rational B-spline | **killed by a 600 s timeout, 2.2 GB RSS**: no result (a hang to the user) |

For comparison `sc_logo.step` (#1536) imports in 1.5 s on the same build.

## Why it is P1

A user-triggered import that runs 10 minutes and 2 GB without an end is the #1536 failure class ("never finishes"). And 13,227 unmatched edges on a 52-face shell of mostly cylinders and cones from a CAD export says the importer meshes these faces wrongly, not that the file is corrupt; #1576's refusal is the safety net doing its job, but it tells the user to re-export a file that is very likely fine.

## Where to look

- The meter from #1546 and the pass-wide budget idea in #1599 bound the time but not the cause.
- The 3 rational B-spline faces per file (`BOUNDED_SURFACE ... RATIONAL_B_SPLINE_SURFACE`) are the likely runaway; the analytic faces should mesh in milliseconds. First step: time each face's tessellation and find which face eats the budget and which faces own the unmatched edges.

## Done means

Both files import closed in seconds (or one names the face it cannot mesh within a bounded time, never minutes), with a fixture that reproduces the runaway (a rebuilt face, not the user's file), pinned by a test.

Found while checking #1574/#1576 against the user's files.

title: 2D Contour and the 2D Pocket wall pass run conventional when climb is true (outside CCW, inside CW with M3)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: P1
labels.description: Unsafe or wrong output: gouge, collision, wrong G-code, crash, data loss; blocks a cut

labels.name: area:2d
labels.description: 2D milling

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Found while programming a simple 2.5D end-cap plate (user's project) with the CamCraft **v0.19.0** release CLI (macOS arm64), driven headlessly over MCP, Tormach PathPilot post. Re-checked on upstream main **d00243a5**: **still reproduces, identical directions**.

## What happens

With `climb: true` (the default, shown in the GUI as "Climb milling"), **2D Contour runs conventional**: with the spindle on M3 the outside profile runs **CCW** around the part and an inside (bore) profile runs **CW**. With `climb: false` it runs the other way, which is the real climb. Every 2D contour posted with the default flag is conventional-milled, silently. In the user's project the three contours had to be set to `climb: false` to get climb.

The **2D Pocket**'s wall pass shares the inversion. Other ops are right:

| Op (`climb: true`, M3) | Measured travel at the floor | Correct for climb? |
|---|---|---|
| 2D Contour, outside | CCW (G3 corners) | **no** (conventional) |
| 2D Contour, inside (bore) | CW | **no** (conventional) |
| 2D Pocket, bore wall pass | CW | **no** (conventional) |
| 2D Adaptive, in the bore | CCW (G3) | yes |
| Bore | CCW (G3) | yes |
| Circular | CCW | yes |

Posted output (main, outside contour, `climb: true`; the part spans X ±50, Y ±30):

```
S9500 M3
...
G01 X50.346 Y-32.98 Z-2 F1200
G03 X53 Y-30 Z-2 I-0.346 J2.98 F1200
G01 X53 Y30 Z-2 F1200
G03 X50 Y33 Z-2 I-3 J0 F1200
G01 X-50 Y33 Z-2 F1200
```

That is the tool going up the +X side and across the top to -X: CCW around the part.

**The convention.** With M3 (clockwise spindle seen from above), climb milling keeps the material on the **right** of the tool's travel (the G41 side): an outside profile runs **clockwise** around the part, an inside profile (a hole or pocket wall) runs **counter-clockwise**. Conventional is the reverse. With M4 both reverse.

**Cause (read, not fixed).** `crates/motion/src/machining2d/contour.rs` (around line 207) says "Canonical orientation is material-on-the-left travel; conventional climbing reverses it", and keeps that order when `p.climb != inside`. Material on the left of the travel with M3 is conventional, so the rule is inverted. The unit test `contour_inside_shrinks_and_flips_travel` in `machining2d/tests.rs` pins the same reading ("climb under Inside travels the loop reversed, so material stays on the left"). The GUI label maps 1:1 to the parameter, so the parameter, not the label, is what is wrong. The pocket's wall pass needs the same check (`pocket.rs` / `pocket_hsm.rs` `plan_passes`); also worth checking 2D Chamfer, Slot, Trace and the contour lead/arc side (`arc_leads.rs` `air_side`), which follow the same flag.

## Minimal repro (MCP)

`plate_bore.stl`: a 100 x 60 x 10 mm plate, centred in XY, z 0..10, with a centred Ø40 through bore.

```
import_model   {"path": "plate_bore.stl", "name": "plate"}
add_setup      {"name": "Setup 1"}
set_stock      {"box": {"dx": 120, "dy": 80, "dz": 12}}
set_wcs        {"stock_point": {"x": "center", "y": "center", "z": "max"}}
add_tool       {"catalog": "EM-0600-4FL", "name": "EM6"}
add_operation  {"kind": "2D Contour", "tool": "EM6", "name": "outside", "source": "plate",
                "params": {"top_z": {"reference": "top_of_stock", "offset": -2},
                           "bottom_z": {"reference": "top_of_stock", "offset": -11},
                           "stepdown": 20, "climb": true, "entry": "plunge"}}
set_operation_geometry {"operation": "outside", "picks": [the 4 top outer edges' chains]}
edit_operation {"name": "outside", "params": {"side": "outside"}}
(same again, "inside", picking the bore's top chain, side "inside")
generate {} ; post {"output": "out.nc"}
```

Result: outside CCW, inside CW (signed area of the floor-level feed moves +7276 / -915 mm²). With `climb: false`: outside CW, inside CCW.

## Expected

`climb: true` with M3: outside profiles CW, inside profiles CCW, on every 2D op that takes the flag (and both reversed under M4), matching Adaptive, Bore and Circular today.

## Done means

- 2D Contour (outside, inside, open chains) and the 2D Pocket wall pass run climb as defined above when `climb: true`, conventional when false; pinned by a direction test per op that checks the signed travel at a level against the spindle direction.
- Every other op with a `climb` flag (Chamfer, Slot, Trace, Face rows, leads) checked against the same rule and pinned.
- The test that pins "material on the left" is corrected, not deleted; affected CL/NC goldens are regenerated in one commit.
- The release notes say that contour and pocket direction changed: a project that set `climb: false` as a workaround will now post conventional.

body:
Found while programming a small two-sided part with HAT-style stock and soft jaws (user's project), with the CamCraft **v0.19.0** release CLI (macOS arm64), driven headlessly over MCP, Tormach PathPilot post.

## What happens

A document with two setups (Setup 1 at G54, Setup 2 at G55, with the part flipped between them) posts as **one program**. Setup 2's first operation follows Setup 1's last move with **no program stop** (`M0`/`M1`) and no message to the operator. From the posted file:

```
G1 X1.3127 Y-1.0908 Z-0.2962 F30
G0 X1.3127 Y-1.0908 Z0.9843
M9
M5
(SETUP: Setup 2)
(OPERATION: S2 Face hat off rough - FACE - G55)
G17 G90 G55 G40 G49 G80
...
T31 M6
G43 H31
S9500 M3
M8
```

On cycle start, the machine finishes Setup 1 and **starts cutting Setup 2's path at once**, before anyone has flipped or re-clamped the part. Setup 2's program is then running on a part still clamped for Setup 1. It cuts air at best; at worst it cuts the wrong side of the part, the vise or the parallels at full feed.

To get one program per setup, the user had to delete the other setup's ops from a scratch copy and post again, or cut the file apart by hand.

A per-operation "after" action already exists (`AfterOperation`: optional stop / program stop / go home, #110), and a program-stop entry can be put after an op in the GUI. **Nothing puts one at a setup boundary by default**, and I found no MCP tool that adds a stop entry.

## Expected

The user chooses, per document (and in the post dialog / MCP `post`), between:

1. **one file per setup** (for example `name_setup1.nc`, `name_setup2.nc`, each with its own header, tool list, work offset and `M30`); or
2. **one file with a stop between setups**: an `M0` (or `M1` if the user prefers) after the last op of each setup, with a comment naming the next setup and what to do (`(SETUP 2: FLIP PART, CLAMP ..., G55)`).

**Safety:** the default for a multi-setup document posted as one file should be the `M0` stop, not "run straight on". A program that moves from one setup to the next with no pause is a crash waiting for an operator who expects it to stop. The current default may deserve a higher priority than this issue carries.

**Done means:** posting a two-setup document either writes one file per setup, or writes one file with an `M0` and a setup-change comment between the setups, as chosen. With no choice made, the default never runs from one setup into the next without a stop. The MCP `post` tool takes the choice. A pinning post test covers both modes on at least the Fanuc and Tormach dialects.

Related: #110 (per-operation after-action), #388 (one file per post when setups use different machines), #258 (post dialog options).

body:
Reported by the maintainer (2026-11-13, in chat, on v0.19.0): "when hovering a "selection" in the geometry tab of an operation it should clearly highlight in the viewwport which you are gonna delete for example.."

What happens: the Geometry tab of an operation lists its selections as rows (for example "Chain Body1 · open · 50.0 mm · 1 of 2", "Face Body1 · z=0.00 · 1250 mm2"), each with a remove button. Hovering a row or its remove button shows nothing in the viewport, so the user cannot tell which edge, chain or face the row stands for before removing it.

Expected: while the pointer is over a selection row (or its remove button), that face, edge, chain or vertex is drawn in the viewport with a strong hover highlight, clearly different from the normal selected style and visible on the shaded and wireframe model in both themes. The highlight goes away when the pointer leaves. The other direction helps too: hovering a selected entity in the viewport marks its row in the list.

This is hover state: immediate-mode only, not a command and not undoable (Everything Is a Command, "Ephemeral UI state"). The UI passes the hovered row to the viewport through the app layer, not by a direct world call from the panel.

Related: issue 1505 (selected edges are too faint; edge picking is unpredictable). The hover style and the selected style should be chosen together.

Done means: a ui test through the test harness hovers a selection row and asserts the viewport's highlighted entity is that row's entity, and none after the pointer leaves; it holds for face, edge/chain and vertex rows; the highlight style is a named constant covered by the structural test; before and after screenshots in the PR.

title: Process changes - fork maintainers please subscribe

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: P?
labels.description: Paused: never picked until the maintainer sets a real priority

body:
**Subscribe to this issue** (the "Subscribe" button on the right) if you work from a fork of CamCraft, especially with an AI agent.

Forks sync product code only at release tags (AGENTS.md "A fork syncs from upstream at each cut tag"). But the *process* - `AGENTS.md`, the agent definitions in `.claude/agents/`, the skills in `.claude/skills/` and `scripts/gate.*` - changes between releases, and a fork's agents should follow the current rules (review labels, priority labels, release steps, and so on).

**How it works:**
- `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` holds one number. Every PR that changes a process file bumps it.
- Every such PR also adds a comment **here**: the new version, what changed, and what to pull. Subscribers get one notification per change.
- A fork's agent compares its `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` with upstream's at the start of each session and, if upstream is newer, pulls just the process files (AGENTS.md "Process files sync on every session"). Product code still waits for the next release tag.

**To pull by hand:**
```
git fetch upstream
git checkout upstream/main -- AGENTS.md .claude/agents .claude/skills .claude/PROCESS_VERSION scripts/gate.ps1 scripts/gate.sh
git commit -m "chore(process): sync process files to upstream PROCESS_VERSION <n>"
```

This issue stays open and pinned. It's labelled `P?` so no agent ever picks it up as work.
